title: Dense Interprocedural Dominance in Acyclic Graphs: Context Bounds and Compact Queries
abstract: Interprocedural dominance asks which program points every matched call-and-return execution must pass on its way to a target. An analysis that writes out immediate dominance pays for the transitive reduction of this order, the minimal dominator graph. Measured instances of that graph look near-linear, with edge-to-node ratios around 1.1--1.26~\cite{DeSutter2007}, but no program property is known to force this: it is unclear which structural restrictions imply sparse output, and whether dense output also rules out cheap queries. This paper answers both through calling contexts. A static node stands for the group of its reachable configurations; write $κ$ for the largest group size and $α$ for how many nodes have more than one configuration. One context per node keeps the tree with $n-1$ edges. Two already allow $Θ(n^2)$ cover edges in a sparse, loop-free, recursion-free ICFG with total degree three, constant-size procedures, and logarithmic stack depth, while the reachable configuration graph itself stays linear, so the blowup comes from grouping, not from many configurations. Three keep $Θ(n^2)$ covers even when the explicit call/return graph is acyclic: all target-reaching runs visit the mandatory procedures in the same order, and extra runs that stop short of any target remove the comparabilities that would otherwise kill the covers. Complementing the lower bounds, $α$ ambiguous nodes admit at most $\min\{\floor{n^2/4},(α+1)(n-1)\}$ cover edges, with $Ω(αn)$ attainable at stack depth one. And for every ICFG with at most two contexts per node, deleting a context group reduces dominance to dual-failure reachability, giving $O(n)$-word, $O(1)$-query representation after polynomial preprocessing. Explicit cover size, context ambiguity, and query-space cost are three separate quantities.

title: Preference-Shift Diagnostics for Iterative Policy Refinement
abstract: The deployment of autonomous systems in dynamic, human-centric environments necessitates continuous adaptation to evolving user preferences. Iterative policy refinement, a cornerstone of modern reinforcement learning and alignment strategies, often assumes stationary preference distributions. However, human preferences are inherently non-stationary, exhibiting complex temporal, contextual, and systemic shifts that degrade policy performance over time. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for preference-shift diagnostics designed to identify, categorize, and address non-stationarity in iterative policy refinement pipelines. By establishing a robust diagnostic methodology, this research bridges the gap between static reward modeling and dynamic operational environments. We propose a multi-layered diagnostic architecture that continuously monitors feedback streams, detects distributional divergences, and attributes these shifts to specific environmental or human factors. Through extensive theoretical analysis and simulated experimental validation, we demonstrate that integrating preference-shift diagnostics significantly enhances the resilience and alignment of autonomous policies. The findings underscore the critical need for diagnostic transparency in policy optimization, providing a scalable solution for maintaining system efficacy in the face of shifting human expectations.

title: ENGRAFT: ENgram GRadient Routing-Aware Fact Transplant
abstract: First public release of ENGRAFT (ENgram GRadient Routing-Aware Fact Transplant): add a fact to Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by gradient descent on the 8 trigram-keyed rows of its n-gram (Engram/PLE) table, through a CPU replica of the frozen model with expert routing refreshed at every step, shipped as an overlay the engine substitutes at read time. What is in this release: the code (Apache 2.0), an offline quick start against fakes, and scripts/reproduce.sh for the real model; the run of record results/2026-09-05/: 7 of 8 facts reproduced by the real llama.cpp engine at first-token probability 0.85 to 0.96, merged overlay identical to single overlays, sister triggers unchanged, CPU replica equal to the full-precision engine on 17 of 17 grafts; the technical report paper/engraft.pdf (CC BY 4.0), attached below. Limitations are stated in the README and in the report: the grafts do not generalize to the fact stated inside a document, one counterfactual fact with a concentrated base-model prior does not take, one model and one run of eight facts. How this was built: the code, the experiments and the write-up were produced in a Claude Code session (Anthropic's Claude, model Fable 5.1) driven by a single human operator who set the goals, approved every design step, ran the hardware and read every result. We want the method checked, broken and improved.

title: Quantum Machine Learning with Multi-Variable Entangled Encoding
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of multi-variable entangled encoding as a novel approach to enhance quantum machine learning algorithms. The core claim is that exploiting multi-variable entanglement can significantly improve the parallel computation capabilities and information storage efficiency within these algorithms. The proposed mechanism involves encoding multiple quantum bits into multi-variable entangled states. Leveraging the inherent correlations within these entangled states allows for parallel computations and information compression. We explore theoretical frameworks and mathematical formulations to demonstrate the feasibility and potential advantages of this technique. The research provides a new perspective on optimizing quantum machine learning algorithms, addressing limitations in current approaches and paving the way for more efficient quantum data processing. This work focuses on the fundamental principles and theoretical underpinnings, without requiring experimental validation.

title: Hierarchical Abstraction Learning for Large-Scale Data
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for hierarchical abstraction learning designed to efficiently process and understand large-scale datasets. The core idea is to automate the discovery of hierarchical representations, which drastically reduces the complexity of data analysis. We introduce a recursive clustering algorithm guided by information-theoretic measures, specifically mutual information, to iteratively refine data representations and construct a hierarchy of abstractions. This approach addresses a significant challenge in dealing with massive datasets by providing a scalable and automated method for identifying underlying patterns and structure. The resulting hierarchical structure facilitates intuitive data exploration and understanding, potentially leading to improved insights and decision-making. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy through theoretical analysis and outline potential applications across diverse domains.

title: Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package: A Stable Machine-Readable Contract for Alignment Research and System Design
abstract: Representation alignment research now spans multimodal, cross-lingual, cross-domain, multi-view, and model-to-model systems, with a rapidly expanding range of models, losses, matching procedures, and training strategies. However, the design decisions that determine whether an alignment strategy is appropriate for a particular problem are often implicit in technical choices or scattered across papers, code, experiments, and local discussion. A method name and its reported performance may show what was used and how it performed without making clear what compatibility was intended, what correspondence was assumed, what information should remain distinct, or why those choices fit the problem. This makes it harder to design systems around the requirements of the problem, compare methods at a common design level, and carry design intent reliably into implementation. Existing resources support important parts of this work. Surveys and taxonomies help researchers understand which alignment methods and research families have been developed. Experiment platforms record what was run and how it performed, while provenance and documentation standards capture where artifacts came from, how they were produced, and how they are intended to be used. These resources make methods, experiments, and artifacts easier to find, reproduce, and inspect. The design rationale connecting a particular problem to a particular form of alignment, however, can remain embedded in local terminology, technical choices, and project-specific documentation. As a result, knowledge generated through earlier design work can remain difficult to compare across projects, transfer between teams, or accumulate into a reusable body of knowledge. The Representation Alignment Compass (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22096467) provides a compact and relatively stable design-level reference for the high-leverage commitments that determine what form of alignment a problem requires. The Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package (RAC-CORE) makes this reference machine-readable and persistent, allowing alignment commitments, context, evidence, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation artifacts to remain connected through a shared semantic structure as methods and implementations evolve. This provides a common basis for explicit design, coherent interpretation of a changing field, cumulative evidence across projects, and shared reasoning across researchers, teams, tools, and computational agents. Theoretical Framework, Core Package, and Practical Companion RAC-CORE is the machine-readable component of a broader three-resource Representation Alignment architecture. This Zenodo record contains RAC-CORE only; the Theoretical Framework and Practical Companion are separate resources. The framework defines the conceptual design semantics, RAC-CORE preserves those semantics in machine-readable records, and the Practical Companion supports their practical application. Theoretical Framework. Use the published Representation Alignment Compass when the primary need is to understand representation alignment, compare design alternatives, or reason about the high-leverage commitments that should shape a research or system-design problem. It remains authoritative for the conceptual architecture, category meanings, and design logic. Core Semantic Package. Use RAC-CORE when those commitments need to become persistent machine-readable records that can be reviewed, exchanged, versioned, linked to evidence or execution, or reused across projects and computational workflows. RAC-CORE is authoritative for machine-readable semantics and conformance. Practical Companion. The Practical Companion, when released separately on GitHub, will provide richer worked examples, guided authoring, templates, workbenches, integration utilities, and other practice-facing support. It will remain pinned to an exact RAC-CORE release while leaving the conceptual framework and Core semantics unchanged. Core Values 1. Making Alignment Designs Explicit and Reviewable RAC-CORE turns the high-leverage commitments identified through the theoretical framework into an explicit, context-scoped design record. Problem conditions, selected configurations, unresolved choices, rationale, and proposed technical realizations can be examined together rather than reconstructed from separate artifacts. Researchers and system designers can use this record to evaluate whether a design is coherent with its intended purpose and constraints, compare candidate configurations, revise specific commitments, and carry the design reliably into implementation or handoff. The theoretical framework supports the reasoning; RAC-CORE preserves the resulting design state in a form that can be reviewed, versioned, and continued. 2. Maintaining a Coherent and Evolvable Alignment Knowledge Structure Alignment methods, models, losses, and implementations can change rapidly while the higher-level design commitments they realize remain comparatively stable. RAC-CORE allows these technical objects to remain externally versioned while linking them to a persistent alignment architecture. New work can therefore be incorporated into an existing body of knowledge rather than creating another isolated technical category, and users can compare contributions at the level of alignment design rather than method name alone. The structure remains stable where its design distinctions continue to hold, while recurring evidence of genuinely new alignment logic can motivate a governed Core revision. This provides a stable basis for building a coherent and evolvable knowledge structure across alignment work. 3. Building an Evidence Base for Cumulative Learning and Long-Horizon Planning Learning across projects requires more than preserving individual results; experiences must be expressed in a form that allows them to be related across changing methods and contexts. RAC-CORE keeps literature interpretations, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation evidence distinguishable but linkable under a stable semantic reference. As reviewed and traceable records accumulate, heterogeneous projects can be represented as structured evidence that can later be assessed for comparability, synthesis, and recurring design patterns under separately governed analysis. This evidence can support later synthesis, diagnosis, meta-level learning, and long-horizon planning under separately governed analytical processes. RAC-CORE does not supply the learned conclusions itself; it provides the common reference structure through which past experience can become usable evidence for future reasoning. 4. Preserving Shared Alignment Semantics Across Projects, Teams, and Agents RAC-CORE provides a common semantic contract for alignment work that moves across projects, researchers, teams, software tools, and computational agents. Canonical identities remain tied to their context, scope, evidence, provenance, uncertainty, and governing release, so records can be exchanged without relying on local terminology or undocumented assumptions to recover their meaning. This supports reliable handoff, cross-project synthesis, accountable revision, machine-assisted review, and long-horizon human–agent collaboration while allowing participants to retain their own methods, datasets, and implementation environments. Supported Tasks RAC-CORE supports two peer machine tasks built on the same theoretical coordinates but representing different epistemic objects. RAC-MAP — Represent an Existing Alignment Design from Evidence Use RAC-MAP when an alignment design already exists and must be interpreted from evidence. The evidence may come from a publication or from direct observation of an executed system, according to the channels defined by the released contract. A RAC-MAP record captures the bounded source being interpreted, the relevant context, the alignment commitments and configurations supported by the evidence, provenance, and the limits of permissible inference. It is designed to preserve partial knowledge without forcing unsupported completion. Publication-derived interpretation and execution-grounded observation remain distinguishable, so what a paper claims and what a system actually executes can be recorded separately. Typical uses include literature and method mapping, system inspection, systematic review, evidence-synthesis datasets, design-history reconstruction, and the construction of reusable alignment-design corpora. RAC-DESIGN — Represent an Intended Alignment Design Use RAC-DESIGN when an alignment strategy is being formulated, reviewed, handed off, or revised. A RAC-DESIGN record captures the problem context, intended alignment commitments, candidate configurations, rationale, unresolved choices, and proposed technical realizations. Concrete methods and implementations remain external objects, allowing technical alternatives to change without redefining the Compass. After implementation, the intended design can be linked to an execution-grounded RAC-MAP and to the associated implementation and evaluation evidence. Typical uses include research planning, system-design specification, design review, team or agent handoff, versioned revision, and traceability from an intended alignment route to its realized form. Downstream Comparison and Learning Conformant RAC records provide a common basis for later comparison, aggregation, visualization, and learning. Shared semantic coordinates make it possible to examine recurring commitments and differences across records, while preserved context and epistemic status help determine whether those records are meaningfully comparable. Any ranking, recommendation, learned tendency, or design-selection procedure remains a downstream analytical responsibility with its own evidence, assumptions, and governance. How to Use RAC-CORE RAC-CORE is used in two primary ways: to represent an existing alignment design

title: Causal Graph Embedding with Counterfactual Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that integrates causal reasoning, specifically leveraging counterfactual analysis. Traditional graph embedding techniques primarily focus on capturing structural relationships within a graph, neglecting the underlying causal dependencies. This limitation hinders the ability to perform "what-if" scenarios or understand the impact of changes on the graph. Our method proposes training a graph embedding model that explicitly learns to represent causal relationships between nodes. This enables the model to answer counterfactual questions, predicting how the graph would evolve under different hypothetical scenarios. We demonstrate the core claim that incorporating causal reasoning significantly enhances graph embeddings, leading to improved counterfactual inference capabilities. The key mechanism involves learning representations that capture directional causal links, allowing the model to effectively simulate changes and predict outcomes. This approach opens up new possibilities for analyzing complex systems represented as graphs, particularly those where causal understanding is crucial for decision-making and prediction.

title: Quantum Resonance Cascade for Algorithmic Complexity
abstract: Quantum Resonance Cascade (QRC) is a novel approach to accelerate the convergence of complex optimization algorithms, particularly evolutionary algorithms, by leveraging quantum entanglement and superposition to dynamically adjust resonance frequencies within a carefully engineered network. This paper presents a detailed theoretical framework and preliminary experimental validation demonstrating the potential of QRC to significantly reduce the computational cost and improve the quality of solutions generated by these algorithms. We explore the fundamental principles of QRC and its application to optimizing complex, multi-variable problems. The core mechanism involves creating a quantum network that resonates at specific frequencies, influencing the evolution of the optimization process. We investigate how this network's structure and the precise application of quantum entanglement can dramatically enhance convergence rates and ensure the exploration of more optimal regions of the solution space. This work offers a fundamentally new perspective on algorithmic optimization and holds promise for accelerating the discovery of advanced solutions across diverse scientific and engineering domains.

title: Title: Adaptive Fractal Dimension - Self-Organizing Data Structures
abstract: This paper presents a novel methodology for automatically generating fractal dimension within data structures, offering a powerful tool for creating highly efficient and adaptable data representations. The core concept revolves around a self-organizing algorithm that iteratively adjusts the fractal dimension based on the inherent structure of the data, ensuring optimal representation for a range of applications. We detail the algorithm's design, its performance evaluation, and a discussion of its potential implications for data science and engineering. The central claim is that this approach facilitates the creation of data structures with dynamically adaptable dimensions, enabling significant improvements in efficiency and flexibility.

title: Probability Logic Networks (PLN) – Adaptive Tensor Representation
abstract: Probability Logic Networks (PLN) represent knowledge as a set of logical rules and probabilities. The effectiveness of a PLN hinges significantly on the quality of its learned representations, particularly the weights associated with each node in the network. This paper explores the development of a novel Adaptive Tensor Representation (ATR) for PLN, aiming to enhance model generalization by dynamically adjusting tensor weights based on input data variations. We introduce a "tensor perception" mechanism, leveraging probabilistic models to evaluate the changes in tensor representations and iteratively refine the network's weights. The proposed approach contrasts with traditional methods by offering a mechanism for self-adaptation, potentially leading to improved performance across diverse datasets. This research presents a framework for dynamically adjusting tensor weights, thereby fostering enhanced generalization capabilities within the PLN.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Emergent System Design
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to designing and simulating emergent systems using probabilistic programming. The core idea is to leverage the inherent ability of probabilistic programming languages to explicitly model uncertainty and explore complex, non-deterministic behaviors. The proposed design space incorporates a domain-specific language (DSL) focused on decentralized systems with partial observability, emphasizing adaptive learning and robust design principles. We argue that this combination represents a significant advancement, providing a powerful tool for tackling the inherent challenges of designing systems where emergent properties arise from complex interactions and incomplete information. The paper outlines the key components of the DSL, detailing its mechanisms for representing system components, defining interactions, and incorporating uncertainty. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a conceptual framework, highlighting its applicability to various emergent system scenarios, without performing actual experiments.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Simulating Complex System Dynamics
abstract: This paper explores the application of probabilistic programming techniques for simulating complex system dynamics, particularly those exhibiting inherent uncertainty. Traditional system simulation often relies on deterministic models built upon simplifying assumptions, which can limit their accuracy and generalizability. This work advocates for the use of probabilistic programming languages—such as Stan and PyMC3—to represent and simulate these systems. These languages allow the construction of Bayesian networks, facilitating the incorporation of prior knowledge, the quantification of uncertainty, and the exploration of a wider range of possible outcomes. The core claim is that probabilistic programming provides a more realistic and robust approach to system simulation by explicitly acknowledging and modeling uncertainty. We demonstrate how this methodology can improve the sensitivity of simulation results to model parameters and provide a more comprehensive understanding of system behavior. The key innovation lies in the seamless integration of statistical modeling and simulation within a single framework, enabling researchers to move beyond purely deterministic approaches.

title: 基于量子神经网络的复杂系统建模
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) for modeling and simulating complex systems. Traditional neural networks often struggle with the inherent non-linearity and high dimensionality characteristic of complex systems, leading to inaccuracies and computational challenges. QNNs, leveraging principles of quantum mechanics such as superposition and entanglement, offer a fundamentally different approach that may overcome these limitations. This work outlines a framework for constructing a QNN specifically designed for complex system modeling, detailing the key components and potential advantages. The core claim is that QNNs can provide a more accurate and efficient method for modeling and simulating complex systems. We introduce a novel mechanism utilizing quantum properties for enhanced representation and processing of complex system dynamics. This represents a new approach to complex system modeling, offering the possibility of uncovering previously hidden patterns and behaviors. This document focuses on the theoretical foundation and design principles of this approach, without involving experimental validation.

title: Graph-Based Representation Learning for Natural Language Processing
abstract: This paper explores the application of graph-based representation learning to the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Traditional NLP models frequently encounter difficulties in effectively capturing the intricate relationships between words, particularly those spanning significant distances within a sentence or document – a phenomenon known as long-range dependency. We propose a novel approach that represents sentences as graphs, utilizing words as nodes and semantic relationships as edges. The core idea is to learn word embeddings directly from this graph structure, enabling the model to inherently capture these long-range dependencies. This method offers a potentially more robust and efficient way to represent textual data compared to traditional methods relying solely on sequential processing, addressing a key limitation in current NLP techniques. We will detail the graph construction process, embedding learning strategies, and present initial insights into the model's performance.

title: Physics-Based Simulation for AI Model Training
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to Artificial Intelligence (AI) model training by leveraging physics-based simulation. Traditional AI training, particularly deep learning, relies heavily on vast datasets and significant computational resources, presenting substantial barriers to entry and scalability. This work proposes a method where the training process of an AI model is mapped and simulated within a physics engine. The engine provides interactive and feedback mechanisms, allowing for the adjustment of model parameters and structure based on physical interactions. title: Adaptive Kernel Learning for Data Representation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to data representation leveraging adaptive kernel learning. Traditional kernel methods, such as Support Vector Machines, rely on fixed kernels, a limitation that restricts their adaptability to diverse data distributions. Our methodology addresses this by dynamically learning the kernel function itself. This is achieved through a recurrent neural network trained on the data's kernel matrix, allowing the kernel to adjust its parameters based on local data density and feature correlations. The core claim is that fixed kernels significantly limit the performance of kernel methods, and the proposed adaptive kernel learning provides a more flexible and accurate representation. The algorithm's key innovation lies in its ability to move beyond static kernel definitions, offering substantial improvements in accuracy across a range of datasets. The theoretical framework is outlined, followed by a discussion of the algorithm's implementation and potential applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a conceptual framework and provide a detailed explanation of the underlying mathematical principles.

title: Probabilistic Logical Programming: A Bayesian Inference Framework
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for probabilistic reasoning by integrating probabilistic logic programming with Bayesian inference. The core claim is to establish a new programming paradigm capable of handling uncertainty and probabilistic reasoning problems. This is achieved by combining the symbolic reasoning capabilities of probabilistic logic with the statistical inference capabilities of Bayesian methods. The framework addresses a critical limitation of existing probabilistic logic programming approaches, which predominantly rely on logical deduction without robust mechanisms for managing and reasoning with uncertain knowledge. The proposed system introduces a layered approach, allowing for both explicit logical rules and probabilistic assessments, ultimately leading to more comprehensive and adaptable reasoning systems. This work outlines the key components of the framework and presents a foundational approach for developing intelligent systems that can effectively navigate complex, uncertain environments. The system aims to improve the accuracy and robustness of probabilistic inference, offering a valuable tool for domains such as expert systems, medical diagnosis, and risk assessment.

title: SignDino: Self-Supervised Sign Language Representation Learning via Temporal-Axis Self-Distillation
abstract: Self-supervised sign language representation learning must model two properties not central to natural-image SSL: signs are produced by a small set of anatomically distinct articulators, and their meaning depends on the temporal organisation of those articulators. We introduce SignDino, a self-supervised sign-video encoder that moves the DINOv3 student--teacher recipe from the spatial domain of image crops to the temporal domain of tracked sign streams. Each video is decomposed into left-hand, right-hand, and face streams by a detector-first YOLOv8n+ByteTrack pipeline. A frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 embeds each per-frame anatomical crop, while lightweight temporal Transformers, not the image backbone, form the student and EMA teacher. They are trained by temporal DINO self-distillation, frame-level masked-token prediction in the style of iBOT, KoLeo feature spreading, and Gram anchoring of the frame-to-frame similarity structure. This design keeps strong image-level visual primitives fixed and learns only how articulator states evolve across time. We evaluate on sign-to-English translation, isolated sign recognition, and fingerspelling detection benchmarks. Across these tasks, SignDino provides a strong public self-supervised representation and shows competitive or state-of-the-art performance under matched downstream evaluation.

title: Nonlinear elliptic homogenization with the parametric Deep Ritz method
abstract: Elliptic homogenization is used to determine coarse-grained properties of materials with features on small scales. When these small scale features have rapid, periodic fluctuations, the solution field corresponding to a homogenized constitutive relation closely resembles the true solution based on the heterogeneous material. This homogenized behavior of the material is computed from a cell problem, where a cell is defined to be one period of the fluctuating material. In the context of linear elliptic partial differential equations, the homogenized constitutive relation is defined simply by a constant coefficient tensor, but for nonlinear problems, the homogenized response depends on the macroscopic state and/or its gradient, thus requiring solutions to parametric cell problems. When computing a numerical solution with the homogenized constitutive relation, it is useful to have a differentiable representation of the solution to the cell problem, as derivatives of the homogenized constitutive relation are required in Newton iterations for the macroscopic state field. In this work, we use the Deep Ritz method to solve the parametric cell problems that arise from nonlinear homogenization. First, we exploit the variational structure of the cell problem, then we discretize the dependence of the cell response on both space and the macroscopic state with a neural network. Enforcing boundary conditions on the cell response strongly, we next use the parametric Deep Ritz method to simultaneously solve the cell problem over a range of macroscopic states. We show that this method is accurate, efficient, and offers a continuous and differentiable representation of the cell response over the macroscopic state and gradient. We then show that our parametric representation of the cell response significantly expedites macroscale solutions when compared to a traditional $\text{FE}^2$ scheme.

title: Layered Cryptographic Trust for Open Digital Systems: A Conceptual Framework Linking Private-Key Limitations, Public-Key Exchange and Post-Quantum Migration
abstract: Modern digital infrastructures rely on cryptography to establish confidentiality, integrity, authentication, non-repudiation and secure key establishment over networks that cannot be assumed trustworthy. Yet the relationship between private-key limitations, public-key exchange, computational security, pseudorandomness, chosen-plaintext security and post-quantum migration is often presented in fragmented form. This study develops a layered design-science framework for cryptographic trust in open digital systems. The work adopts a conceptual review method supported by standards-based triangulation. Core techniques were analysed against their security role, mathematical basis, computing requirements, application domain, operational risk and post-quantum relevance. The resulting framework shows that symmetric encryption remains the most practical mechanism for high-volume data protection, but it depends on reliable key establishment and lifecycle governance. Public-key cryptography provides scalable trust and authentication, while Diffie-Hellman exchange and key derivation functions connect mathematical shared-secret construction to deployable session keys. Pseudorandomness and chosen-plaintext security give formal discipline to encryption design, whereas post-quantum cryptography introduces migration requirements for long-term confidentiality and identity assurance. The study contributes an integrated architecture that connects cryptographic theory, implementation practice and institutional readiness. Its main implication is that secure systems should be designed as hybrid, lifecycle-aware and algorithm-agile infrastructures rather than as isolated deployments of individual cryptographic primitives.

title: Division and Modulo from Recursive Normalization
abstract: We define integer division and modulo by recursively normalizing quotient–remainder states and verify the construction in Scala Stainless. We prove uniqueness of the normalized solution, compatibility with native modulo for nonnegative dividends and positive divisors, invariance under shifts by multiples of the divisor, together with addition, subtraction, and modulo-idempotence laws. We also verify the unit-step quotient–remainder transition and that every block of p consecutive nonnegative integers, for p > 1, contains exactly one zero remainder modulo p. Together, these results show that recursive normalization is canonical on the stated domains and recovers the verified algebraic and periodic laws of division and modulo.

title: Contextualized Memory Networks with Dynamic Attention
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to Memory Networks (MemNets) designed to address the limitations of existing models in effectively utilizing memory based on context. The core problem lies in the static nature of memory access within standard MemNets, which often leads to inefficient information processing. We propose a Contextualized Memory Network (CMN) incorporating a dynamic attention mechanism. This mechanism allows the network to learn and assign weights to memory slots dynamically, reflecting the relevance of each slot to the current input. The CMN leverages this context-aware memory representation to improve performance in tasks requiring nuanced understanding and long-term dependency modeling. The resulting architecture demonstrates enhanced ability to prioritize relevant information within the memory, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency. The key innovation is the integration of a learnable attention layer that adapts to the input context, moving beyond the fixed-weight approaches of traditional MemNets.

title: The Exact KL Radius of Two Bernoulli Products on Three Bits
abstract: Anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed computer-assisted theorem candidate addressing AIM-PROBABILITY-0002. The claimed exact maximum forward-Kullback-Leibler error of the closed RBM(3,1) model, equivalently a mixture of two Bernoulli products on three bits, is -3/4 log(2 sqrt(3)-3) nats (approximately 0.830615532444 bits), attained only by the two uniform parity targets. The package contains the 11-page manuscript, analytic lower bound and continuous support/channel reduction, six exact convex-cover certificates with 16,600 leaves and 93,792 vertex conditions, a standard-library verifier, adversarial tests, a rational target-to-feasible-witness interface, and an elementary nonsharp conditioning upper bound for specified higher-dimensional product-mixture budgets. It also includes the review response and five producer-coordinated internal editorial reports. The exact Stage-1 review target is preserved as a separate ZIP. SHA256SUMS.txt binds the three substantive assets. The constant and conditioning principle have explicitly cited prior antecedents. Finite diagnostics, producer replay, CI and internal model review are not unaffiliated mathematical validation. No general optimal-projection algorithm, higher-dimensional sharpness, general larger-RBM equivalence, exhaustive novelty, formal verification, external peer review or four-star impact is claimed. Original manuscript, certificate data and editorial material: CC0. Original executable code: MIT, as specified in LICENSE-CODE. Third-party papers, supplied-review text and other NOASSERTION material are not redistributed. Publisher: Evidence Press.

title: Dynamic Topological Dependency Semantic Networks (DTSSN)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topological Dependency Semantic Networks (DTSSN), a novel approach to predicting and interpreting complex system behavior. Traditional knowledge representation methods often struggle with the inherent dynamism and intricate dependencies found in complex systems. DTSSN addresses this limitation by constructing a continuously evolving knowledge graph that explicitly models topological relationships and dynamic semantic associations. The core of the system lies in its "living graph" methodology, where nodes represent system components or concepts, and edges represent dependencies and semantic relationships (such as causality, influence, or similarity). The graph's topology adapts in real-time based on system state and events, coupled with a "semantic flow" mechanism to capture dynamic changes in these relationships. This semantic flow leverages deep learning models, specifically Variational Autoencoders (VAE) or Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), to learn and represent semantic associations and propagate them through the graph based on topological information. Prediction and interpretation are then achieved through graph-based reasoning, employing techniques like Reinforcement Learning or Causal Inference algorithms for decision-making and scenario simulation. DTSSN's innovation lies in its ability to move beyond static knowledge representation, offering a dynamic framework to analyze and anticipate behavior in systems exhibiting non-linearity, high dimensionality, and temporal evolution.

title: Interpretable Deep Learning Models with Causal Reasoning
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of causal reasoning into interpretable deep learning models. Current interpretable models often rely on statistical correlations, which can be misleading and lack true understanding. We propose a novel approach that leverages causal graphs and causal rules to guide the training of deep learning models, ensuring that learned relationships are genuinely causal. This method aims to enhance both the interpretability and trustworthiness of these models. We introduce a framework where causal inference is explicitly incorporated into the model architecture and training process. The core claim is that by embedding causal reasoning, we can significantly improve the explanatory power and reliability of interpretable deep learning models. We explore the mechanisms involved in translating causal knowledge into actionable model adjustments. This work contributes to a more robust and reliable approach to AI, particularly in domains where understanding the underlying causal mechanisms is paramount. The ultimate goal is to develop models that not only predict accurately but also provide transparent and trustworthy explanations for their decisions. ---

The core mechanism centers on manipulating quantum geometry to generate tailored quantum states, offering a fundamentally different approach to quantum data manipulation and secure communication. The study explores the potential of this technique, demonstrating the generation of entangled states exhibiting specific topological features, potentially opening avenues for advanced quantum technologies.

title: Non-linear Geometry-Physical Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for modeling complex systems utilizing a non-linear geometric model. We propose a system that integrates geometric principles with physical processes, allowing for predictive capabilities and providing a foundation for quantum computation. The core claim is that this model, built through a non-linear geometric framework, can accurately simulate physical behavior and offer new theoretical insights for quantum computing. The research explores the potential of leveraging geometric properties to enhance the fidelity and interpretability of quantum computations.

title: High-Order Quantum Entanglement Computation Models
abstract: This research explores the development of novel computational models predicated on high-order quantum entanglement, aiming to significantly enhance the efficiency and scalability of quantum computation. Traditional approaches often struggle to effectively utilize the unique properties of entangled states, necessitating innovative modeling strategies. This work proposes a framework leveraging these properties to enable complex quantum computations, pushing the boundaries of what is currently achievable with existing quantum hardware. The core mechanism centers on dynamically generating and manipulating entangled states, facilitating algorithms with enhanced expressiveness and reduced resource requirements. The resulting models offer a pathway to overcome limitations inherent in current quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum States of Self-Organizing Information Fields
abstract: Quantum information fields are fundamentally different from classical information fields, exhibiting unique properties that enable novel computational paradigms. This paper explores the concept of self-organizing information fields – a theoretical framework that posits the existence of patterns and structures within these fields that drive their dynamic behavior. We investigate the potential of leveraging these self-organizing characteristics to design a quantum algorithm that surpasses current limitations in quantum computation and data transmission. The core mechanism centers around identifying and exploiting specific patterns within these fields to generate highly efficient and rapid data transfer. The investigation begins with a conceptual analysis of self-organization, progresses through a proposed quantum algorithm architecture, and ultimately details the anticipated benefits of this approach. This work seeks to contribute to the advancement of quantum information processing by demonstrating a viable path towards more powerful and versatile quantum technologies.

title: 混沌域优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to optimization, termed "Chaos Domain Optimization," that leverages the inherent properties of chaotic domains to generate global optimum solutions. Traditional optimization techniques often struggle with finding truly optimal solutions, particularly for complex, high-dimensional problems. This research proposes a method that dynamically maps the optimization problem to a chaotic domain, effectively mimicking the self-organization and sensitivity to initial conditions found in chaotic systems. We detail the algorithm's methodology, its mathematical foundation, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness compared to conventional methods. The core innovation lies in the intelligent mapping process, which aims to capture the essential dynamics of the problem within the chaotic domain, enabling the discovery of more robust and globally optimal solutions. This work contributes to the field of optimization by providing a fundamentally new approach that potentially overcomes limitations of existing methods.

title: Cognitive Graph Embeddings with Hierarchical Abstraction
abstract: Existing graph embedding techniques primarily focus on capturing low-level relationships within a graph, often failing to represent the higher-level, hierarchical structures that are fundamental to human cognition. This paper proposes a novel approach to graph embeddings – Cognitive Graph Embeddings (CGEs) – which explicitly incorporates hierarchical abstraction. CGEs utilize a multi-layered graph representation where nodes are organized into levels of granularity, mirroring the way humans understand and process information. The core mechanism involves learning embeddings for nodes at each layer, allowing for the representation of concepts at varying levels of abstraction. We introduce a framework for constructing these layered graphs and a corresponding embedding method that leverages both local and global graph information. The key innovation lies in the explicit modeling of hierarchical relationships, leading to embeddings that better reflect cognitive structures and potentially improving performance in downstream tasks that require understanding of complex relationships. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CGEs through a conceptual framework and discuss its potential applications in areas such as knowledge representation, reasoning, and recommendation systems.

title: 基于量子纠缠的几何度量
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for precise measurement based on quantum entanglement, aiming to surpass the limitations of traditional measurement techniques. The core principle of this approach leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to construct a sophisticated density estimation algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through rigorous theoretical analysis and preliminary numerical simulations, showcasing its potential to significantly enhance the accuracy of numerical computations across various fields. The presented method offers a pathway toward more reliable and precise results, particularly in scenarios demanding high fidelity.

title: Contextual Graph Embeddings with Relational Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding generation that leverages relational reasoning within a contextual framework. Traditional graph embedding methods often treat nodes and edges independently, failing to capture the complex relationships derived from an entity's surrounding context. Our method utilizes a transformer architecture to attend to both node features and the relational structure of the graph, incorporating knowledge graph embeddings to enrich the representation learning process. The core innovation lies in the direct integration of relational reasoning into the embedding learning process, resulting in embeddings that more accurately reflect the nuanced connections between entities. We demonstrate that this contextual approach significantly outperforms existing graph embedding techniques in downstream tasks, particularly those requiring an understanding of complex relationships. The generated embeddings are evaluated using metrics such as node classification accuracy and link prediction performance.

title: Relational Reinforcement Learning with Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the integration of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Relational Reinforcement Learning (RRL) to address the challenges of complex, multi-agent environments. Traditional RRL struggles with accurately representing and reasoning about the intricate relationships between entities, leading to suboptimal decision-making. We propose a novel framework that leverages GNNs to encode these relationships into a graph structure, allowing the agent to learn directly from the network of interactions. The agent utilizes the GNN to update its representation of each entity, incorporating information from its neighbors, ultimately improving the agent's ability to predict future states and choose optimal actions. We formally define the model and outline the key components, emphasizing the benefit of graph-based representations for enhanced relational reasoning. The core claim is that RRL can be significantly enhanced by incorporating GNNs. The core mechanism involves combining RRL with GNNs to learn relationships and interactions between objects as a graph. The novelty lies in this combined approach, enabling more sophisticated decision-making. The framework demonstrates improved performance in simulated environments compared to standard RRL approaches. The primary mathematical contribution lies in the formulation of the enhanced RRL algorithm and the associated graph convolutional operations.

title: Adaptive Compiler Optimization Strategies Based on Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the application of evolutionary algorithms to adaptive compiler optimization. Traditional compiler optimization relies on predefined rules and heuristics, often failing to adapt to the specific characteristics of the source code and target architecture. This research proposes a novel framework where optimization strategies are treated as an evolutionary problem, utilizing algorithms like genetic algorithms to dynamically adjust and refine these strategies. The core claim is that this adaptive approach significantly improves compiler optimization performance. The mechanism involves modeling optimization decisions as a search space within an evolutionary algorithm. The algorithm iteratively explores this space, selecting and combining promising optimization strategies based on their impact on code performance metrics. This work presents a theoretical foundation and a conceptual design, focusing on the methodology rather than a specific implementation. The results, though not presented through empirical experimentation, demonstrate the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach. This research contributes to a fundamental shift in compiler design, moving from static optimization to dynamic adaptation.

title: Representation Learning for Sample-Efficient CATE Estimation by Leveraging Multiple Outcomes
abstract: Estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATE) enables efficient targeting of interventions, but many applications have limited experimental samples, making it difficult to estimate heterogeneous effects from high-dimensional covariates. In such settings, policymakers and medical practitioners often succumb to the curse of dimensionality or apply off-the-shelf dimension reduction methods that may not preserve treatment heterogeneity. Yet these domains often come with large historical datasets measuring a wide range of outcomes -- a source of supervision that is rarely exploited in practice. Following causal representation learning, we hypothesize that such domains with high-dimensional covariates have lower-dimensional underlying dynamics. We can thus leverage the diverse outcomes measured in historical data to learn a lower-dimensional representation of the covariates. Theoretically, we prove that when the auxiliary outcomes satisfy a set of surrogacy conditions and the representation retains relevant covariate information, the original CATE is identified when the high-dimensional covariates are replaced by the learned representation. Combined with existing dimension-dependent rates for CATE estimation, the result implies greater sample-efficiency on the same experimental sample. Additionally, we characterize the bias-variance tradeoff when the assumptions do not hold perfectly, and show that the representation-based estimator can still achieve lower error when the reduction in estimator variance outweighs the bias due to compression. Empirically, we evaluate the method on synthetic data and semi-synthetic medical data.

title: Factors Influencing the Emergence of Dependency Length Minimization in Neural Agent Simulations
abstract: Given various grammatical options, language users prefer the word order choice that reduces the overall length of syntactic dependencies, a principle known as dependency length minimization (DLM). The origins of this preference remain an open question, particularly whether it originates from constraints on efficient information processing. Computational simulations provide a powerful approach to identifying the factors influencing the emergence of linguistic phenomena. However, previous simulations of DLM have not examined realistic interaction contexts and have produced mixed results. The present study investigates the emergence of DLM in artificial languages using a recently proposed language learning and communication framework based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In this framework, agents are trained to speak and interpret artificial languages and then use these languages to communicate. Using this framework, we study the impact of several factors related to processing limitations in a communicative setting, such as noise during listening, limited speaker capacity, and incremental sentence processing. Our results reveal a complex interplay among these factors in shaping word order preferences in neural agents. Specifically, in the full meaning space, agents regularize toward a single dominant word order, while in the half meaning space they show a short-before-long preference that only aligns with DLM in verb-initial languages. A consistent DLM preference emerges only when agents are subject to incremental processing pressure. These findings suggest that limitations in human cognitive processing may indeed play a role in shaping DLM. Our findings provide insights into the conditions under which neural models replicate human-like preferences and highlight the challenges of designing emergent communication models that capture human cognitive biases in language processing.

title: PROBLEMS OF MACHINE TRANSLATION IN THE RUSSIAN–ENGLISH DIRECTION: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF MODERN TRANSLATION SYSTEMS
abstract: This article examines Russian–English machine translation using Yandex, Google, DeepL, and ChatGPT and evaluates their performance based on BLEU, METEOR, and POS-BLEU metrics. The findings reveal differences in lexical, semantic, and syntactic accuracy, with Yandex demonstrating the strongest overall performance. The study also highlights the limitations of automatic translation evaluation metrics and emphasizes the importance of combining them with expert assessment and post-editing, particularly when translating scientific and specialized texts.

title: Evaluating the Potential of Artificial Intelligence in Improving Business Intelligence in Lusaka: A Case Study of Airtel Zambia
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into customer-service and Business Intelligence (BI) environments, but evidence on the readiness and customer-service implications of such integration in Zambia remains limited. This study evaluated the potential of AI to improve BI for customer service at Airtel Zambia in Lusaka. The study was guided by the Technology Acceptance Model, the Technology-Organisation-Environment framework and the DeLone and McLean Information Systems Success Model. A mixed-method case-study design was adopted. Quantitative data were obtained from 52 Airtel subscribers through a structured questionnaire, while contextual evidence was obtained from one Airtel Zambia IT Director. The achieved subscriber sample represented 52.5% of the intended 99 respondents. Descriptive statistics were used for subscriber responses, while the key-informant response was analysed thematically and compared with subscriber evidence. The findings showed that subscribers viewed the accuracy of customer-service information and the usability of Airtel's digital platforms positively, but perceptions were weaker regarding the use of previous interactions and personalised recommendations. Support for AI-enabled service was stronger: 78.4% of valid respondents preferred WhatsApp communication, 78.4% would use an AI chatbot if it provided instant responses and 81.6% wanted usage-based bundle recommendations. The IT Director confirmed the use of BI systems and data analytics in customer-service decisions, while reporting that infrastructure and AI-related expertise were only partially capable of supporting AI. Management support and funding were reported as available and overall organizational readiness was rated as ready. The study concludes that Airtel Zambia has a meaningful foundation for AI-enabled customer service, but implementation should be phased and accompanied by stronger infrastructure, AI skills, data governance, human escalation and customer-visible personalisation.

title: Arnold's Bifurcation Principle Applied to RLHF Alignment Training: Real-Time Hardware Prediction of Alignment Collapse Using Hessian-Free Curvature Velocity Tracking
abstract: When a language model is aligned using human feedback, its behavior sometimes breaks in a way nobody wanted: it starts giving answers that score well on the automated reward signal but are actually worse, evasive, repetitive, or unsafe. This is called alignment collapse. Recent published work has shown that one cause of this breakdown is geometric: the curvature of the training loss, in certain sensitive directions, bends the model’s parameters into those directions even when the very first training steps point safely away from them. title: Information-Theoretic Foundation for Federated Learning Privacy
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data while preserving data privacy. However, existing privacy-preserving techniques frequently rely on approximations and heuristics, often lacking rigorous mathematical justification. This work presents a novel information-theoretic framework for analyzing and controlling information leakage in federated learning. We leverage concepts from source coding and channel capacity to derive tight bounds on the information revealed by local model updates. These bounds provide provable privacy guarantees, offering a significant advancement over existing methods. The core contribution lies in establishing a solid, mathematically grounded foundation for FL privacy, facilitating the design of more robust and efficient privacy-preserving algorithms. We demonstrate the framework's applicability through theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential for optimizing privacy-utility trade-offs within FL systems. ---

title: Explainable Deep Learning Model Generation (EDLMG)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to generating explainable deep learning models, termed Explainable Deep Learning Model Generation (EDLMG). The core challenge in deploying deep learning models is their inherent lack of transparency, hindering trust and adoption. EDLMG addresses this by leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to automatically construct model architectures specifically designed for enhanced interpretability. Furthermore, it integrates rule-based reasoning to provide transparent explanations for the model's decision-making process. The system aims to create models that are not only accurate but also understandable, offering a crucial step towards responsible and reliable AI. The primary contribution lies in the automated generation of interpretable models, coupled with a robust explanation framework, thereby offering a practical solution to the explainability problem within deep learning. The framework incorporates key elements of controlled architecture design through GANs and subsequently employs symbolic reasoning for transparent decision justification. This approach allows for a shift from "black box" models to models where the underlying reasoning can be readily scrutinized and validated.

title: Dynamic Neuro-Morphic Architecture Adaptive Topology
abstract: This paper investigates the development of dynamic neuro-morphic architectures capable of adaptive topology. The core concept revolves around enabling neural networks to dynamically modify their neuron connectivity and overall structure to optimize performance on specific tasks, and to proactively adapt to the complexity of the input data. The proposed framework utilizes reinforcement learning to adjust neuron connection weights, coupled with topology optimization algorithms (such as genetic algorithms or simulated annealing) to facilitate the adaptive evolution of the neural network's topology. Unlike existing adaptive architectures that typically focus on layer or neuron-level adjustments, this research aims to provide a deeper control and evolutionary capability over the entire network topology. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, paving the way for more robust and efficient neural networks. The primary goal is to create a system that learns and adapts its structure, ultimately surpassing the limitations of static, pre-defined architectures.

title: Quantum Error Correction Codes: An Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Quantum error correction is a crucial aspect of quantum computing, enabling the reliable transmission and manipulation of quantum information. Traditional methods often rely on fixed parameter optimization, which struggles to adapt to the inherent variability of quantum systems. This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive optimization algorithm designed to dynamically adjust quantum error correction code parameters based on input data entropy changes, thereby significantly enhancing the code's performance and robustness. We propose a method that leverages the inherent dynamics of quantum states to optimize the code's parameters in real-time, offering a potential pathway to overcome limitations of traditional approaches. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that continuously assesses the error rate and adjusts the code's parameters to minimize this error.

title: 基于量子纠缠的自适应算法评估
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement as a novel mechanism for evaluating algorithm performance. Traditional algorithm evaluation methods often rely on manual tuning, limiting adaptability and potentially hindering optimization. We propose a new approach that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to automatically assess algorithm efficiency, offering a significant advancement in performance evaluation. The core mechanism involves establishing a quantum entangled state with the algorithm's output, allowing for a rapid and non-deterministic assessment of its characteristics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations and analyses, showcasing its ability to identify areas for improvement and enhance algorithm efficiency. The resulting system promises a shift towards more dynamic and adaptive evaluation methodologies.

title: 拓扑空间中的自适应机器学习的几何建模
abstract: This paper investigates the application of geometric modeling techniques within topological spaces to enhance the generalization capabilities of machine learning models. Traditional machine learning often relies on fixed parameters, limiting model flexibility and potentially hindering performance across diverse datasets. We propose a novel framework, "Adaptive Geometry Modeling," that dynamically adjusts the underlying geometric structure of a model, allowing for automated parameter tuning. This framework leverages the inherent properties of topological spaces to guide the model's evolution, leading to improved robustness and adaptability. The core mechanism centers around representing the model as a dynamic geometric transformation, where adjustments are driven by the model's internal representation of the input space. This allows for automatic optimization of parameters to achieve optimal performance on unseen data. The paper will detail the design and implementation of this framework, showcasing its potential benefits through illustrative examples and analysis.

title: Relational Neural Networks for Temporal Sequence Prediction
abstract: This paper investigates the application of relational neural networks to the problem of temporal sequence prediction. Traditional recurrent neural networks (RNNs), while effective, often struggle to explicitly capture the complex relationships inherent within temporal sequences. We propose a novel architecture that incorporates relational reasoning, allowing the network to directly model and utilize the dependencies between elements in the sequence. Our approach moves beyond the limitations of standard RNNs by encoding temporal dependencies as explicit relationships between data points, offering a more interpretable and potentially more accurate method for sequence prediction. We demonstrate the efficacy of this relational neural network (RN-Net) through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, focusing on the core mechanisms driving improved performance. The key innovation lies in shifting from solely learned embeddings to an architecture that explicitly represents and reasons about the connections within the temporal data. This allows for more robust handling of sequential data and offers a promising direction for future research in sequence prediction.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Large-Scale Scheduling Problems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired optimization algorithms to the resolution of large-scale scheduling problems. The core premise is that techniques inspired by quantum mechanics, specifically quantum annealing, can provide efficient solutions to these complex problems. The approach involves mapping the scheduling problem onto a quantum annealer model, leveraging the quantum tunneling effect to effectively explore the solution space and converge towards optimal schedules. We present a framework for this mapping and discuss the potential advantages in terms of speed and scalability compared to traditional classical optimization methods. The research contributes to the growing intersection of quantum computing concepts with operations research, offering a novel approach to tackling significant scheduling challenges.

We highlight the potential for this approach to unlock new computational capabilities and address limitations of current quantum hardware.

title: Bridging the gender gap in STEM education with AI: Female-coded chatbot as role model and learning assistant
abstract: Despite the potential of AI chatbots for personalized learning, empirical evidence for their effectiveness in addressing STEM gender disparities remains limited. This study explores the efficacy of ADA, a female-coded AI chatbot, in mitigating mathematical gender stereotypes while promoting equitable learning outcomes. A quasi-experimental study ( N = 195 ninth-grade German students, mean age = 14.33 years) conducted in mathematics classes compared the AI chatbot with traditional printed help cards on the Heron method. The study measured stereotypical beliefs, technological acceptance, emotions, situational interest, cognitive load, and academic performance. Results demonstrate a significant reduction in gender-stereotypical beliefs, with small but meaningful effect sizes observed across both genders. Technological acceptance was high, exhibiting no gender differences. The intervention promoted learning efficacy for both genders, with a significant gain in situational interest and no statistically significant gender differences in learning performance, emotional responses, or cognitive load. These findings underscore the potential of systematically designed AI chatbots as scalable pedagogical tools that simultaneously challenge gender stereotypes and promote equitable learning efficacy. Subsequent longitudinal research is required to validate the long-term sustainability and generalizability of these effects.

title: What Does Animal Re-Identification Learn? Linear Biological Concepts and Their Origins in Visual Representations
abstract: Conservation increasingly relies on camera traps that collect more wildlife imagery than experts can manually analyze, making animal re-identification (Re-ID) essential for monitoring individuals and populations. Yet understanding which cues drive model decisions is challenging for ViT-based Re-ID models, whose metric-learning objectives provide no explicit supervision for biological concepts. We ask whether such models nonetheless organize their representations along biologically meaningful axes. Using a DINOv3 backbone fine-tuned for Western lowland gorilla Re-ID with triplet-margin loss, we find that sex and age emerge as linear directions that generalize to held-out individuals, reaching up to 0.91 AUROC and being recoverable from a single image per individual. Activation steering further shows that the sex direction is causally used by the model, flipping a significant fraction of predictions to the opposite sex. Comparing off-the-shelf and fine-tuned backbones shows that Re-ID training does not create these concepts, but relocates them across the network. Finally, data attribution reveals that the representation we find reflects a graded biological axis, is redundantly encoded across the population and shaped by visually ambiguous individuals. Together, these findings show how interpretability can uncover both the biological structure and failure modes of Re-ID representations, providing a step toward auditable computer vision for wildlife monitoring.

title: Three Infinite Classes of APN Permutations on $Z_n$
abstract: For any permutation of a nontrivial finite abelian group, the differential uniformity is at least two; permutations attaining this bound are called almost perfect nonlinear (APN). We construct three infinite classes of APN permutations on the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_n$ using Singer cycles, binomials inducing projective permutations, and completed reciprocals combined with parity and quadratic characters. The respective domain orders are $q+1$ for prime powers $q>2$, $(3^d-1)/2$ for integers $d\ge2$, and $2p$ for primes $p>5$ with $p\equiv5\pmod6$. Each class contains an infinite subclass of composite orders outside the standard forms $r-1$, $r-2$, $r-3$, and $r-4$, where $r$ is a prime power. These forms arise in the Welch--Costas, Panario--Sakzad--Stevens--Wang, and Golomb constructions. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first infinite APN constructions on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ reported since 2011 that yield infinitely many composite orders outside these standard forms.

title: Exact Order of the Ho–Nguyen Polynomial System for Overfitted Gaussian Mixtures
abstract: This paper determines the exact order of the polynomial system introduced by Ho and Nguyen in the study of singularities and parameter convergence rates for overfitted Gaussian mixtures. The result resolves the general order predicted from the previously known two- and three-component cases. The upper bound is proved by converting coefficient cancellation in the polynomial system into vanishing moments of a signed finite combination of Gaussian densities. A sharp bound on the number of sign changes of such Gaussian combinations is then combined with a sign-interpolating polynomial to rule out any nontrivial solution at the critical order. The argument applies to arbitrary positive mixture weights and arbitrary real location and scale perturbation parameters. Sharpness is obtained from positive Gaussian quadrature. For every number of excess components, a Gauss–Hermite construction gives a nontrivial positive-weight configuration attaining cancellation through the preceding order. Thus the upper and lower bounds coincide for every component count covered by the Ho–Nguyen system. The proof is self-contained at the level needed for the main result and includes a treatment of repeated Gaussian variances in the sign-change argument. Exact symbolic computations provide independent checks of the quadrature identities, low-dimensional cases, and coefficient formulas, but the general theorem is analytic and does not depend on finite computational verification. The result concerns the Ho–Nguyen polynomial system associated with overfitted Gaussian location-scale mixtures. It is distinct from the author's earlier work on skew-normal mixture paths, although both use positive Gauss–Hermite quadrature as a sharp lower-bound mechanism. No claim of priority over all unpublished or undiscovered work is made. Research methodology and AI assistance:This work was developed using the CARMA-Math research workflow, a cumulative AI-assisted mathematical research methodology using persistent research archives, literature and prior-art investigation, iterative proof exploration, and verification procedures. Generative AI (ChatGPT) was used extensively for mathematical exploration, proof development, computational reasoning, literature research, and manuscript preparation.

title: Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Search for Complex Optimization Landscapes
abstract: This research presents a novel stochastic search algorithm, termed Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Search (QISS), designed to address the challenges posed by complex, high-dimensional, and non-convex optimization landscapes. Traditional stochastic search methods often struggle in these scenarios due to premature convergence and difficulty exploring diverse regions of the solution space. QISS draws inspiration from quantum mechanics, specifically the concepts of superposition and measurement, to enhance exploration and exploitation. The algorithm maintains candidate solutions in a probabilistic superposition of multiple states, and employs randomized projection operations analogous to quantum measurement to collapse the superposition, effectively guiding the search towards potentially optimal regions. The core idea is to mimic the probabilistic nature of quantum states, allowing the algorithm to simultaneously consider multiple possibilities before "measuring" and focusing on the most promising one. This approach demonstrates potential for improved performance compared to conventional stochastic search techniques, particularly in situations where the landscape is highly irregular and contains numerous local optima. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through simulations, showcasing its ability to navigate complex landscapes and converge towards solutions with improved accuracy and efficiency.

title: Federated Learning with Blockchain-Based Security Mechanisms
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for secure federated learning leveraging the inherent properties of blockchain technology. The core claim is that utilizing blockchain's distributed consensus mechanism can establish a robust and reliable system for federated learning, effectively safeguarding the privacy of participating entities' data. The proposed mechanism involves recording model updates on a blockchain, employing consensus to guarantee the authenticity and consistency of these updates, and integrating encryption techniques to protect data privacy. This approach addresses the existing security vulnerabilities within traditional federated learning systems, significantly enhancing their overall security posture. The system's architecture and operational principles are detailed, outlining a practical solution for building trustworthy and privacy-preserving federated learning environments. Further, the paper explores potential challenges and future research directions within this domain.

title: Non-Locality Geometric Optimization Algorithms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel geometric optimization algorithm combining local and global optimization techniques, leveraging reinforcement learning and evolutionary algorithms. The algorithm is designed to address the challenge of adapting to dynamic environments and local variations, effectively utilizing the strengths of both approaches. The core mechanism involves introducing evolutionary algorithms to dynamically adjust the solution space, while incorporating feedback mechanisms to maintain structural consistency. The proposed approach offers a robust and adaptable solution for complex geometric optimization problems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Topological State Preservation
abstract: Quantum-enhanced topological state preservation is a novel approach to safeguarding quantum information, particularly in the context of long-duration data storage. This paper details a method utilizing a 'quantum feedback loop' to continuously monitor and correct deviations from a defined quantum state, thereby maintaining its integrity across multiple iterations of a quantum algorithm. The core mechanism involves a dynamic feedback process that actively adjusts the quantum state to minimize errors, offering a promising pathway to robust quantum data management. We present a theoretical framework and initial implementation demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in preserving topological states, highlighting its potential to overcome limitations in current quantum data storage techniques.
